entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14346"/><div sID="gen27791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14346"/><hi type="bold">5. Master--</hi>betokening not surely a first acquaintance, but a relationship already formed.<div eID="gen27791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all night--</hi>the usual time of fishing then (<reference osisRef="John.21.3">Joh 21:3</reference>), and even now Peter, as a fisherman, knew how hopeless it was to "let down his net" again, save as a mere act of faith, "at His word" of command, which carried in it, as it ever does, assurance of success. (This shows he must have been already and for some time a follower of Christ.) <div eID="gen27792" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14355"/><div sID="gen27809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14355"/><hi type="bold">30. their scribes--</hi>a mode of expression showing that Luke was writing for Gentiles.<div eID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.5.33-Luke.5.39">Lu 5:33-39</reference>. Fasting.</title> <div sID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.9.14-Matt.9.17">Mt 9:14-17</reference>.)<div eID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The incongruities mentioned in <reference osisRef="Luke.5.36-Luke.5.38">Lu 5:36-38</reference> were intended to illustrate the difference between the genius of the old and new economies, and the danger of mixing up the one with the other. As in the one case supposed, "the rent is made worse," and in the other, "the new wine is spilled," so by a mongrel mixture of the ascetic ritualism of the old with the spiritual freedom of the new economy, both are disfigured and destroyed. The additional parable in <reference osisRef="Luke.5.39">Lu 5:39</reference>, which is peculiar to Luke, has been variously interpreted. But the "new wine" seems plainly to be the evangelical freedom which Christ was introducing; and the old, the opposite spirit of Judaism: men long accustomed to the latter could not be expected "straightway"--</hi>all at once--to take a liking for the former; that is, "These inquiries about the difference between My disciples and the Pharisees," and even John's, are not surprising; they are the effect of a natural revulsion against sudden change, which time will cure; the new wine will itself in time become old, and so acquire all the added charms of antiquity. What lessons does this teach, on the one hand, to those who unreasonably cling to what is getting antiquated; and, on the other, to hasty reformers who have no patience with the timidity of their weaker brethren! <chapter eID="Luke.5"/>
